title: The Unfaithful Wife and the New Betrothal
summary: Speaking as a wronged husband, the LORD brings charges against Israel, who has gone after Baal and credited him with her grain, wine, and oil. He will block her way, take back his gifts, and end her festivals. Then the tone turns: he will lead her into the wilderness, speak tenderly to her, and betroth her to himself forever in righteousness, justice, loving devotion, compassion, and faithfulness, reversing the names of judgment from chapter 1.
story: Chapter 1 told the story of Hosea's household; chapter 2 tells the story it stood for. The speaker is now mostly the LORD, and the unfaithful wife is Israel, called the mother of the children, who are the Israelites themselves. The lines between Hosea's family and God's people blur on purpose. The chapter looks back to Israel's beginnings, the exodus and the wilderness, when she followed the LORD in the days of her youth (verse 15), and it looks forward past judgment to a renewed covenant. It is the fullest statement of the book's message and the source of language later prophets and the New Testament would use for God's love for his people.
historical:
The chapter fits the prosperity of Jeroboam II's reign in the first half of the eighth century BC. Israel enjoyed good harvests, silver and gold, festivals, and trade (verses 5, 8, 11), and many credited that plenty to Baal. The worship of Baal had been promoted at court a century earlier by Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kings 16:31-33) and opposed by Elijah on Mount Carmel, in a contest over who sends rain (1 Kings 18). Jehu had later purged Baal's temple in Samaria (2 Kings 10:18-28), but Hosea shows that Baal worship, or a blend of it with the worship of the LORD, persisted among the people. Inscriptions and personal names from the period confirm how common that blending was. Administrative receipts found at Samaria from the eighth century include personal names built on Baal alongside names built on the LORD's name, and inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud in the Sinai, from around 800 BC, invoke the LORD of Samaria together with his Asherah, which many scholars take to be a goddess treated as his consort, or her sacred symbol.

The threat that God will take back his grain, wine, and wool and turn the vineyards to thicket was fulfilled in the Assyrian invasions of the 730s and the fall of Samaria in 722 BC. The Valley of Achor (verse 15) was the site near Jericho where Achan was executed for taking forbidden plunder from Jericho, the first city of the conquest (Joshua 7:24-26); its name means trouble.
cultural:
Baal was the storm god of the Canaanite world, known from texts found at Ugarit on the Syrian coast. He was believed to bring the rain that made crops grow, and his worship was bound up with the farming year. Hosea insists that the grain, new wine, and oil (the three staple crops of the land) and the wool and linen came from the LORD all along (verse 8). The word baal also meant master, owner, or husband in ordinary speech, so an Israelite could call the LORD my baal without meaning anything pagan. Verse 16 ends that ambiguity: Israel will call God my husband (ishi), not my master (baali), and the names of the Baals will be forgotten.

The imagery of verses 2-13 draws on the legal and social customs of marriage in the ancient Near East. A husband could divorce an adulterous wife and send her away without the provision he owed her, and public stripping as a sign of disgrace is a picture Jeremiah and Ezekiel also use (Jeremiah 13:26; Ezekiel 16:37-39). A husband was obliged to provide for his wife (Exodus 21:10 names food, clothing, and marital rights); God threatens to withdraw what he had given. Betrothal, by contrast, was a binding engagement sealed by a payment from the groom's family. In verses 19-20 God pays the bride price himself, in righteousness, justice, loving devotion, compassion, and faithfulness.
literary: The chapter is poetry built on a threefold therefore. Each therefore (verses 6, 9, and 14) follows a charge and introduces what God will do. The first two are acts of judgment: hedging her in with thorns and taking back his gifts. The third, where the reader expects the harshest penalty, is a surprise: I will allure her and lead her to the wilderness, and speak to her tenderly. From there the chapter piles up promises marked by in that day or on that day (verses 16, 18, 21). The closing verses form a chain of response: God answers the heavens, the heavens the earth, the earth the grain and wine and oil, and they answer Jezreel. The last verse gathers all three children's names from chapter 1 and reverses each of them.

outline.t: The charge against the unfaithful mother
Her way blocked: she did not know who gave her plenty
The gifts taken back and the festivals ended
Wooed in the wilderness: my Husband, not my Master
The covenant of peace and the betrothal forever
Heaven and earth answer, and the names are reversed

doctrines.note: Israel's sin is that she does not acknowledge who gave her grain, wine, and oil, and credits Baal instead. Idolatry often means treating God's gifts as though they came from somewhere else, and pursuing the gifts rather than the giver.

God pictures his covenant with Israel as a marriage, and its renewal as a betrothal forever. The new covenant is founded on God's own qualities, righteousness, justice, loving devotion, compassion, and faithfulness, which he brings to it as a bride price.

Rain, harvest, wool, and linen come from the LORD, not from the powers people imagine are in charge of nature. The chapter ends with creation itself answering in harmony when God's people are restored.

God's discipline blocks Israel's path so that she will say, I will return to my first husband (verse 7). Judgment is meant to bring her home, and the wilderness becomes a place of new beginning rather than only punishment.

words.note: Baal, the Canaanite storm and fertility god, and also an ordinary word for master, owner, or husband. Hosea plays on both senses. Israel has chased the Baals (the plural covers local forms of the god worshiped at many shrines), and in the renewed covenant even the word will be removed from her lips (verse 17).

Ish, man or husband. In verse 16 Israel will call God ishi, my husband, instead of baali, my master. Both words could mean husband, but ish carries the sense of a personal partner rather than an owner. The shift describes a relationship of intimacy and loyalty, not only authority.

Aras, to betroth, to pledge a woman in marriage by paying the bride price. Repeated three times in verses 19-20, it describes a new beginning, as if God will start the marriage over again, not merely patch it up.

Hesed, loving devotion, loyal covenant love. It is one of the five gifts God brings to the betrothal in verse 19, alongside righteousness, justice, compassion, and faithfulness. Hosea will later complain that Israel's hesed is like morning mist (6:4); here God supplies what she lacks.

christ: The chapter's movement from judgment to betrothal anticipates the New Testament's picture of Christ as the bridegroom of his people. John the Baptist calls Jesus the bridegroom (John 3:29), Jesus speaks of himself the same way (Mark 2:19-20), and Paul describes the church as a bride betrothed to one husband, Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2). The Bible ends with the marriage of the Lamb and a bride made ready (Revelation 19:7; 21:2). Paul quotes verse 23 (with 1:10) to show God calling people who were not his people, Jews and Gentiles alike (Romans 9:25-26). Hosea's promise that God will abolish bow and sword and make his people lie down in safety (verse 18) belongs to the prophets' hope for a covenant of peace, which Christians see begun in Christ and completed in the new creation. The one who pays the bride price in Hosea is God himself; the New Testament says he paid it in his Son.

hard.q: How should we read the harsh images of stripping and exposure in this chapter?
hard.a:
Verses 3 and 10 threaten to strip the unfaithful wife and expose her, and many modern readers find these lines painful, especially readers who have experienced abuse. Several things help in reading them honestly. First, the chapter is a metaphor about a nation. The wife is Israel as a people, and her lovers are Baal and the foreign powers she trusted; the stripping describes what invasion and famine would do to the land, left bare like a desert. Second, the images come from the legal customs of the ancient world, in which public shaming of an adulteress was known, and prophets used their culture's language to make the seriousness of covenant betrayal felt. Third, the chapter does not stop there. Its turning point is the wilderness, where God speaks tenderly, restores what was lost, and makes a new covenant.

Scholars differ on how much weight to give the problem. Some, including many feminist interpreters, argue that the metaphor, whatever its intent, has shaped harmful attitudes and should be read critically. Others stress that the text describes God's judgment on a nation and never authorizes any husband to treat a wife this way. Both groups agree that using this passage to justify the mistreatment of women is a grave misuse. The Bible elsewhere commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church, giving himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25).

questions: Israel did not acknowledge who gave her grain and oil. What good gifts in your life are you tempted to credit to something other than God?
God says he will allure Israel into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her there. Has a hard season ever become a place where you heard God more clearly?
The chapter distinguishes calling God my Husband from calling him my Master. What is the difference in how you relate to God?
